chapter_theme: Honour (மானம்): those who have it burn at the arrogance and contempt of the rich, will not lay their need before the unworthy, keep away from patrons who demean them, and would rather die, or refuse heaven itself, than incur sin, blame or loss of honour. Honour is set in a scale of what people fear and is said to bring good in this world and the next.
structure_note: The chapter frames honour through the honourable poor man's relation to the rich (291-293, 296, 298-299), between general statements of its worth (294) and of choosing death over blame (295, 297), and ends with the tiger that will not eat what falls on its left (300). 291 and 298 are a pair, both comparing the honourable mind to fire.

291.reading: Whenever they see the arrogance of the worthless, whose only strength is their wealth, the minds of men of honour blaze like fire raging through a forest.
291.nuance: The fire is inward: the verse says the mind burns, not that they act on it. Mudaliar quotes a definition of மானம் as not falling from one's station and not living on when brought low by fate.

292.reading: Will those who own themselves follow the graceless to tell of their plight, even if they waste to bone? Will they not tell their pain to the clear-sighted, who grasp it before it is spoken?
292.nuance: Honour here does not forbid asking; it chooses whom to ask. The right patron reads the need before it is said, so the honourable never have to beg in words.

293.reading: We would bring our guests into our homes, but they, as if their wives' chastity would be lost if we so much as saw them, shame-faced, set rice before us at the back door; so forget the friendship of the rich.
293.nuance: Both commentators take the poor speaker as one who would let his wife serve guests, while the rich hide theirs and feed the poor at the back. Mudaliar notes another reading in which இல்லம் is simply the house and கற்பு is firmness.

294.reading: Girl with hair fragrant with musk, see how good it is, the esteem of men of honour: it does good in this life and, never leaving the right way, yields good things in the next.
294.nuance: Honour is justified by its fruit in both worlds, which makes it a part of virtue rather than pride. Mudaliar glosses மதிப்பு as the principle men of honour hold, and notes another reading: being well regarded by others.

295.reading: The worthy will not do what brings sin and blame, even if they must die: death is the pain of one day, one moment, and nothing does such lasting harm as those.
295.nuance: The argument is a calculation of duration: death's pain is brief, sin and blame's are not. Mudaliar separates them: sin follows one into later lives, blame stays in this world.

296.reading: Among all who live in this rich, wide world, those who do not give are poor even if they are rich; and those who, even in poverty, do not go and beg from the rich are the great Muttaraiyar.
296.nuance: பெருமுத்தரையர் is a name of liberality: Mudaliar takes them as generous patrons of the author's time, also named in an earlier quatrain, and Shanmuganar as a royal line; Pope translates the name as 'lords of the three mighty lands'.

297.reading: Girl of long dart-like eyes under wide bow-brows: the lowest all fear burning hunger, the middle fear hardship, and the highest fear only the blame in people's words.
297.nuance: A scale of persons by what they fear. Shanmuganar adds what follows from each fear: the lower will do anything, the highest refrain from wrong.

298.reading: When the rich look down on them and say with contempt, 'good people, very kind, now poor', the minds of the foremost worthy may burn within like fire blown in a smith's forge.
298.nuance: The insult is disguised as praise. Both commentators take அளியர் as kind or compassionate, and Shanmuganar makes the kindness the cause of the poverty; Pope takes it as pitiable, 'in greatly reduced circumstances'. Mudaliar glosses எற்றி where the verse has எள்ளி.

299.reading: Not giving to those who come wanting is no shame, and shrinking each day from fear is no shame; the shame, when one is reduced by want, is to leave unspoken what one's superiors did to one.
299.nuance: What the superiors did is left unnamed, so the verse can mean either keeping silent about their slights or failing to acknowledge their help, and the sense of நாண் shifts with it. Mudaliar gives both readings; Pope takes it as not daring to tell their injuries.

positions.position: His main reading: what the richer did is the slight they showed, which one does not speak of; he also reports the reading that one fails to proclaim their help.
The greatest shame is failing to speak gratefully of help one's superiors gave in one's poverty.

300.reading: The forest tiger that has killed a great beast will starve to death rather than eat it if it falls on its left; so the excellent would not want even wide heaven placed in their hands if it came at the dulling of their honour.
300.nuance: Both commentators take கடமா as the elephant (Mudaliar also gives wild cow) and இடம் வீழ்ந்தது as falling on the left, citing a Purananuru poem on the tiger's custom; Pope reads a wild cow and carrion fallen in its path. Heaven itself, not just wealth, is refused.

links.note: Both make the honourable mind a fire lit by the rich: a forest fire at their arrogance (291), a forge fire at their contemptuous pity (298).

Both refuse 'going behind' those who scorn (Kural இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று, here இயல்பிலார் பின்சென்று). The Kural says it brings neither praise nor heaven; 292 says the honourable go to those who understand unasked.
Both allow asking before the right people: the Kural finds a beauty in asking those of open heart who know their duty, and 292 sends the honourable to those who grasp the need before it is spoken.
Kural 1057 delights in givers who give without scorn; 293 shows the giver who feeds the poor at the back door with contempt, and draws the matching conclusion: forget such friendship.
Both set an absolute limit: the worthy will not do what brings blame, not to save a starving mother (Kural) and not to save their own lives (here).
Both say the rich who do not give are poor and the poor who do not beg are rich. 296 adds a name for the honourable poor, the great Muttaraiyar.
Both make fear of blame the mark of the highest: the Kural's பழிநாணுவார் see a millet-sized fault as a palmyra; here only blame frightens the best, while lower people fear hunger and pain.
Each book gives honour an animal that dies rather than compromise: the yak that will not live once its hair is gone (Kural), the tiger that starves rather than eat prey fallen on its left (here).
Kural 966 says that following those who scorn you does not lead to the gods' land. 300 goes further: even if heaven were in hand, the excellent would refuse it at honour's cost.

source_issues: Quatrain 295: the verse reads சாயினும் where Mudaliar glosses சாவினும்.
Quatrain 296: Shanmuganar's field begins with the stray word துன்பவியல், a section heading.
Quatrain 300: Mudaliar glosses அழுங்க where the verse has மழுங்க, and Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
